question: Which song by The Beatles starts with a chord jump from the tonic to the minor fitfh chord?

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The opening that is normally quoted in this connection is the one that is most often described as a tonic – tritone/“minor-fifth’’ leap, the opening of *Come Together*.

In the recording the band is set up in E, the tonic E major being stated by the rhythm guitar and the drums. The first melodic/bass statement of the riff is heard against that E tonic and the immediately-sensed harmonic reference is the v/ bV area – the E–Bb/G# tritone idea that is the basis of the famous Come Together riff. In the literature the move is routinely glossed as the Beatles’ I → ♭V / minor-fifth jump, the E tonic being left behind for the tritone-related minor-fifth sonority that colours the whole introduction.

The same I–v minor fifth movement is the one that is most often cited in the rock-theoretical literature for the White Album’s *Helter Skelter*, the song being introduced in E major/minor with the E tonic slammed straight into the B minor v chord, E → Bm, i.e. a tonic to the minor fifth-degree chord jump, the classic I → v opening that is normally quoted as the Beatles’ textbook tonic-to-minor-fifth jump.

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Norwegian Wood (This Bird Has Flown). The song opens in E major, and the first harmonic move is from E major (the tonic, I) to B minor (the minor fifth, v). You can hear it in the opening acoustic progression and in the first vocal phrase: “I once had a girl” sits over E, then “or should I say” shifts to B minor. That I–v jump is the chord movement the question describes.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The opening that music-theorists point to as the Beatles’ textbook I – b5 / I – tritone jump is the first section of *Happiness Is a Warm Gun* from The White Album.

The song is written in C major. The vocal entry ‘I need a fix…’ is introduced over a tonic C major triad and is immediately answered by a jump up a tritone to the chord whose root is a minor fifth above the tonic, the F♯/G♭ area that in the recording is heard as a F♯ major/minor colour. In conventional terms that is I → bV, the tonic to the minor-fifth / tritone substitution, the very dissonant I–bV leap that gives the opening its characteristic ‘wrong’ jump. The same tritone-dominant colour is reused throughout the first verse/chorus section of the track and is the move most often cited as the Beatles’ famous tonic-to-tritone opening.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The opening that is normally quoted for this effect is the one that everybody cites for a very odd first two bars, “Strawberry Fields Forever”. 

In the studio version the song is heard in A major / A minor and the famous intro is heard as an A-major tonic sonority that is immediately answered by the tritone-flattened fifth of the key, the E♭-major / G♭-major area which is the A–E♭/G♭ tritone/minor-fifth root movement I – bV. The opening A–E♭ leap is the textbook Beatles I → minor-fifth / bV tritone jump that is usually described as a tonic-to-the-minor-fifth-chord opening. The effect is the same one that is often discussed for the very similar Helter Skelter / I Am the Walrus style tritone openings, with Strawberry Fields Forever being the canonical Sgt. Pepper-era example.

10.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’d answer “Norwegian Wood (This Bird Has Flown).” The song is in E major, and the opening moves from the tonic E chord to B minor—the minor chord built on the fifth degree (v). The guitar establishes E, then the vocal line shifts to Bm on “Or should I say,” giving that tonic-to-minor-fifth jump right at the start.

5.text:
The jump that is usually quoted in that vocabulary is the I – v opening that the group used on its late-’63 / early-’64 number one material.

The classic textbook example is the E major / B minor opening that you hear on
*Norwegian Wood – This Bird Has Flown* / *I Feel Fine* material.  In the key the
song is heard in the sitar / guitar intro is set up on the tonic E major and the
first real harmonic move of the verse is a big root-fifth lift to the v-chord,
B minor, E → Bm.  That is the tonic-to-the-minor-fifth-degree I → v jump that is
quoted as the Beatles’ characteristic “tonic-to-v” opening; the same I → v
gesture is the one that is normally talked about in connection with Help! /
I Feel Fine / A Hard Day’s Night.  In the conventional teaching version the
exemplar most often cited is the Norwegian Wood / I Feel Fine opening, E
major → B minor, i.e. tonic → the minor-fifth-degree chord.

3.text:
The jump that is usually quoted is the white-album C – G♭ tritone that opens
‘I Want You (She’s So Heavy)’, and the same material is quoted in the
introduction to ‘Happiness Is a Warm Gun’.

In the key of C the very first sounding harmony is the tonic C major.
The next harmony that is brought in against it is the G♭-major/minor
sonority a diminished 5th / minor 5th – i.e. a tritone – away from C.
C → G♭ is the classic tonic-to-♭5 / tonic-to-minor-5th root motion
C–G♭ = six semitones, the minor fifth/tritone, which gives the song its
characteristic abrupt, heavy opening. The same C–G♭/I–♭V motion is the
one that is normally cited for the ‘Happiness Is a Warm Gun’ intro.

That is the form in which the I → v minor-fifth move is most often taught:
in the major-key songs the familiar I–v minor-fifth move is the A–E m
opening of, e.g., ‘I Saw Her Standing There’/‘Can't Buy Me Love’, A
major tonic followed immediately by the v minor E minor.

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The textbook Beatles I → v / tonic-to-minor-fifth opening that is
always quoted is the one everybody knows as the opening of A Hard Day’s
Night.

In the key the number is usually quoted as G major. The number 1
harmony that you hear at the very first down-beat is G, the tonic of the
song.  The next harmony that the rhythm section lands on is the v chord
in the same key, E minor – the minor triad built on the fifth degree of
the tonic, the ‘minor fifth’ chord.  The characteristic leap of the
bass / guitar from G down a perfect fifth to E, i.e. tonic → minor fifth,
is the jump that gives the song its instantly recognisable opening
gesture.

The same kind of tonic-to-flat-V / tritone leap is the one that is
normally illustrated with Come Together, the song famously opening in
E with the tonic E immediately answered by the flat-V / minor-fifth
area of the harmony, the E → B♭/B♭m- colour that the John Lennon bass
riff is built on, and which is the Beatles’ classic textbook instance of
the tonic → minor-fifth / tritone jump.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The textbook tritone/I–bV opening that is always quoted in connection with the Beatles is the G → E♭ opening of the verse of A Day In The Life, the 1967 I–♭V jump that is normally described as a tonic-to-minor-fifth / tonic-to-tritone jump.

In the popular discussion the same kind of tonic-to-v / tonic-to-the-minor-fifth-degree opening is normally illustrated with the very obvious I–v opening of the early rock-and-roll numbers, e.g. I Saw Her Standing There/All My Loving in the key of A/G, the song is stated in the tonic A/G major and the first harmonic move is down to the v chord, E minor/ G minor, i.e. the minor triad built on the fifth degree of the tonic.  It is that I→v move that is the Beatles’ canonical “tonic to the minor-fifth chord” opening and it is most often quoted with All My Loving/I Saw Her Standing There, and in the later canon with the I–♭V tritone version of the verse of A Day In The Life / Come Together, G major → E♭ major, the tonic to the flattened fifth/minor fifth of the tonic.

8.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The classic textbook example is the opening of A Hard Day’s Night.

In the key the song is heard in, G major, the number one guitar figure that opens the
record is a tonic G – G6 – G quintal sound and it is answered immediately by the
minor v of the key, D minor, i.e. the root of the second harmony lies a perfect
fifth / a minor–fifth chord quality above the tonic root. It is that G → Dm/I → v
jump, heard as the famous “hard day’s” two-chord hammer that is quoted over and
over again as the Beatles’ most conspicuous tonic-to-minor-fifth opening.

The same I → v opening is the one that is normally illustrated on Revolver with
the E-major → B-minor opening of And Your Bird Can Sing, E major being the tonic
and B minor the diatonic minor v of E major, the same tonic-to-minor-fifth
intervallic gesture in a different key.

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The deliberation is split on what “tonic to the minor fifth chord” is meant to denote, and that ambiguity is driving the divergence.

* Tritone / I→bV reading: Several colleagues treat “minor fifth” as a tritone, i.e. tonic to the flat-five chord.
  - Come Together is the most repeatedly cited tritone example: quoted as E major tonic → Bb / G# / bV area, E–Bb tritone jump.
  - Happiness Is a Warm Gun / I Want You (She’s So Heavy) is quoted as C major → Gb/F# , C→Gb tritone, with Colleague 3 and 4 pointing to White Album I→bV material.
  - Strawberry Fields Forever is quoted as A → Eb / Gb, A→Eb tritone, Colleague 2.
  - A Day in the Life verse is quoted as G → Eb, I→bV, Colleague 9.

* I→v reading: Several colleagues treat “minor fifth chord” as the minor triad built on the fifth scale degree, i.e. a perfect-fifth root motion I→v.
  - Norwegian Wood (This Bird Has Flown) is the most consistent I→v citation: E major tonic → B minor v, Colleagues 10, 7, 5. The same E→Bm move is also claimed for Helter Skelter by Colleague 1.
  - A Hard Day’s Night is claimed by Colleagues 6 and 8 as G → Em / Dm, I→v, with some disagreement on whether it is Em or Dm.
  - And Your Bird Can Sing is noted as E→Bm I→v, Colleague 8.
  - All My Loving / I Saw Her Standing There is cited as A/G → E/Gm I→v, Colleague 9.

Errors / tensions I have noted:
- E→Bm is a perfect fifth root motion, not a minor-fifth/tritone interval; colleagues conflating I→v with a “minor fifth interval” are mixing interval size with scale-degree quality.
- Come Together’s opening is often described as a tritone, not a diatonic v.
- A Hard Day’s Night opening is disputed among colleagues as Em vs Dm and whether it is truly an immediate chord jump.
Changes in belief: I started with no prior. After round 0 I see two competing families of answers. If the question intends the tritone / bV sense, Come Together and Happiness Is a Warm Gun / I Want You are the strongest canonical candidates, with Come Together being the most repeatedly named. If the question intends the diatonic v sense, Norwegian Wood E→Bm is the most consistently named single song, with Helter Skelter a close secondary.

Unresolved: Which definition of “minor fifth chord” the question setter uses – tritone flat-five vs minor triad on the fifth degree – and therefore which candidate is correct. Need clarification on interval vs scale degree.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion is split between two readings of “tonic to the minor fifth chord”.

* I → v interpretation – tonic to the diatonic minor triad built on the fifth degree.  
  * Norwegian Wood / This Bird Has Flown is repeatedly cited as E major → B minor, E → Bm at the start of the verse / on “or should I say”. Colleague 10, 5, 7 push this.  
  * Same I → v gesture is claimed for And Your Bird Can Sing E → Bm, Colleague 8; for Helter Skelter E → Bm, Colleague 1; for A Hard Day’s Night G → Em and also G → Dm versions, Colleagues 6, 8; for I Saw Her Standing There / All My Loving / A Hard Day’s Night A/G → E/Gm, Colleague 9.  
  * The I → v family is the one most often taught as the Beatles’ “tonic-to-minor-fifth-degree” opening.

* I → bV / tritone interpretation – tonic root a minor fifth / tritone away.  
  * Come Together is given as the canonical tritone opening, E tonic → Bb / G# area, I → ♭V. Colleague 1, 6.  
  * I Want You (She’s So Heavy) / Happiness Is a Warm Gun are given as C → Gb / F#, I → ♭V. Colleague 3, 4.  
  * Strawberry Fields Forever is given as A → Eb / Gb, I → ♭V. Colleague 2.  
  * A Day in the Life is given as G → Eb, I → ♭V. Colleague 9.  

Notices / errors: Colleague 8’s A Hard Day’s Night claim is inconsistent – G → Dm is not v in G major, v is Em; Colleague 4’s Happiness Is a Warm Gun description conflates F# with Gb, but the root motion is tritone. Colleague 6 mixes I → v and I → ♭V examples in the same argument.

No consensus yet. The tritone reading makes Come Together/I Want You/Happiness Is a Warm Gun the strongest textbook cases; the diatonic minor-fifth-degree reading makes Norwegian Wood/And Your Bird Can Sing/Helter Skelter the strongest textbook cases. I need a definitive identification of the opening harmony for the candidate songs to resolve which root motion actually occurs at bar 1.

5.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question is ambiguous between two readings of “tonic to the minor fifth chord”: 
1) I → v, a diatonic move from tonic to the minor triad built on the fifth scale degree, i.e. a perfect fifth root movement; 
2) I → bV / tritone, a root movement of a diminished/minor fifth ~ six semitones / tritone.

Round 0 shows a clear split between those readings.

Tritone / I→bV camp:
* Come Together is repeatedly cited as the canonical E tonic → Bb / bV tritone leap, described as E tonic set up then the E–Bb/G# tritone riff. Colleague 1 also links Helter Skelter to the same idea.
* Strawberry Fields Forever is claimed as A major tonic → Eb major / bV tritone jump.
* I Want You (She’s So Heavy) / Happiness Is a Warm Gun is claimed as C tonic → Gb major / bV tritone, Colleague 3 and 4 both stress C→Gb as the textbook I → bV / minor-fifth root motion, with Colleague 4 describing Happiness Is a Warm Gun as C → F#/Gb.
* A Day In The Life is cited by Colleague 9 as G → Eb, an I–bV tritone verse opening.

I→v diatonic minor-fifth-degree camp:
* Norwegian Wood (This Bird Has Flown) is the most repeated single answer: E major tonic → B minor, v. Colleagues 10, 5, 7 give the same E→Bm description, with 5 also linking I Feel Fine material.
* A Hard Day’s Night is repeatedly put forward for I→v, but with inconsistent spelling: Colleague 6 says G → Em, Colleague 8 says G → Dm, both described as tonic to the minor fifth-degree chord. The exact second chord is disputed in the room.
* And Your Bird Can Sing is mentioned by Colleague 8 as E major → B minor, the same E→Bm I→v gesture as Norwegian Wood.
* Colleague 1 also notes Helter Skelter as E → Bm, i.e. I→v.

Evidence problems / disagreements noted:
* Definition of “minor fifth chord” is not settled; some colleagues use it for the tritone bV, others for the diatonic v chord.
* The A Hard Day’s Night second chord is described as both Em and Dm by different colleagues.
* Norwegian Wood’s immediate harmonic move is asserted as E→Bm, but the intro guitar is often described as E–A…; the timing of the first vocal change needs verification.
* Come Together’s opening is described as tonic E then Bb tritone, versus Helter Skelter as E→Bm.

Current belief: I cannot yet commit to a single song. The strongest consensus for a textbook tritone opening is Come Together, E→Bb. The strongest consensus for a textbook diatonic I→v opening is Norwegian Wood, E→Bm, with A Hard Day’s Night also heavily cited. Unresolved is the precise definition intended by the question and the exact first two harmonies in the recordings for the top candidates. Need to verify actual first measures of Come Together, Norwegian Wood, A Hard Day’s Night, and Happiness Is a Warm Gun before finalising.

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question is being interpreted in two different ways by colleagues, and the answers diverge accordingly.

Interpretation A – tonic → v, i.e. a tonic chord followed immediately by the diatonic minor triad built on the 5th degree, a perfect-fifth root movement with a minor-quality chord. 
* Colleague 10, 5, 7 argue for Norwegian Wood (This Bird Has Flown) in E major: E → Bm on the opening vocal / guitar statement.
* Colleague 6, 8 argue for A Hard Day’s Night, variously described as G → Em and G → Dm, i.e. G major tonic to the v of the key.
* Colleague 6 and 8 also cite And Your Bird Can Sing as a Revolver example of E → Bm.
* Colleague 5 links the same I→v gesture to I Feel Fine / Help! / A Hard Day’s Night material.
* Colleague 1 cites Helter Skelter as E major/minor → Bm v opening.

Interpretation B – tonic → ♭V / a minor-fifth / tritone root jump, i.e. a 6-semitone / diminished-fifth interval from tonic.
* Colleague 1, 6 cite Come Together in E with the E tonic followed by the E–B♭/G# tritone/minor-fifth area, described as I → ♭V.
* Colleague 2 cites Strawberry Fields Forever as A major/minor tonic answered by E♭/G♭, A → E♭ I → ♭V tritone jump.
* Colleague 3, 4 cite the White Album C–G♭ tritone that opens I Want You (She’s So Heavy) and is quoted for Happiness Is a Warm Gun. Colleague 4 describes Happiness Is a Warm Gun as C major → F♯/G♭, i.e. I → ♭V.
* Colleague 9 cites A Day In The Life verse G → E♭ and also links Come Together/Come Together-style I–♭V.

Notable disagreements / errors:

reflection_text.9:
Round 0 public input is dominated by two different interpretations of “tonic to the minor fifth chord”.

Interpretation A – I → v, tonic to the diatonic minor chord built on the fifth degree, a perfect-fifth root motion with a minor triad quality.
Interpretation B – I → ♭V / I → tritone, tonic to a chord whose root is a diminished/minor fifth / six semitones above the tonic.

Interpretation A claims repeatedly:
* Norwegian Wood (This Bird Has Flown) in E major, E → Bm, I → v, cited by Colleagues 10, 5, 7.
* A Hard Day’s Night in G major, G → Em / Dm, I → v, cited by Colleagues 6, 8. Colleague 8 also claims G → Dm, Colleague 6 claims G → Em; the exact second chord is disputed.
* And Your Bird Can Sing, I Feel Fine / I Saw Her Standing There / Can’t Buy Me Love, A major / G major I → v, cited by Colleagues 5, 8, 9.
* Helter Skelter E → Bm, cited by Colleague 1.

Interpretation B claims:
* Come Together, E tonic → Bb / G# tritone area, I → ♭V / minor-fifth interval, cited by Colleagues 1, 6.
* Strawberry Fields Forever, A tonic → Eb / Gb tritone, I → ♭V, cited by Colleague 2.
* I Want You (She’s So Heavy) / Happiness Is a Warm Gun, C tonic → Gb / F# tritone, I → ♭V, cited by Colleagues 3, 4. Colleague 3 explicitly links the C → Gb move to both I Want You and Happiness Is a Warm Gun.
* Happiness Is a Warm Gun, C → F# / Gb, I → ♭V, with the same C–Gb motion noted by Colleague 4.
* A Day In The Life, G → Eb, I → ♭V, cited by Colleague 9.

Errors / inconsistencies noticed so far:
* Colleague 8’s G → Dm for A Hard Day’s Night is a fourth, not a fifth.
* Colleague 6 simultaneously cites A Hard Day’s Night G → Em and Come Together E → Bb as the textbook I → minor-fifth jump, conflating I → v with I → ♭V.
* Multiple songs are being conflated: Helter Skelter, Come Together, I Feel Fine, Norwegian Wood are all invoked for the same I → v gesture.

My current belief is that the phrase “minor fifth chord” is being used in the literature most often for the tritone / ♭5 root motion, not the diatonic v. If that reading is correct the canonical examples are Come Together, Happiness Is a Warm Gun / I Want You, Strawberry Fields Forever, all I → ♭V tritones. Come Together is the most repeatedly quoted as the Beatles’ textbook I → ♭V opening.

The unresolved question is whether the question setter means a diatonic v minor chord a perfect fifth away, or a tritone ♭V minor-fifth interval. The evidence in round 0 leans toward the tritone reading being the intended one, with Come Together and Happiness Is a Warm Gun / I Want You as the leading candidates, while Norwegian Wood / A Hard Day’s Night represent the competing I → v reading.

2.text:
The split in round 0 is real and it is exactly the “minor fifth” wording that creates it.

If the phrase is taken in interval terms – a root motion of a minor/diminished fifth, i.e. a tritone, tonic → ♭V – then the Beatles textbook example that is repeatedly cited is the opening of *Come Together*.

The band is set up in E. The riff and the bass are heard against an E major tonic and the first harmonic colour that is brought in against it is the tritone related area E → B♭/G♯, the I → ♭V / minor-fifth root motion that underpins the whole introduction. That is the move that is normally glossed in the literature as the Beatles’ I → ♭V ‘tonic-to-minor-fifth’ jump, and it is the same family of move that is quoted for *Happiness Is a Warm Gun* / *I Want You (She’s So Heavy)*, C → G♭/F♯, and for the A → E♭ tritone opening of *Strawberry Fields Forever*.

If instead “minor fifth chord” is taken in scale-degree terms, i.e. the minor triad built on the fifth degree of the major key, I → v, the most consistently named single song in this round is *Norwegian Wood (This Bird Has Flown)*. The number is heard in E major and the first real harmonic move of the verse is E major → B minor, tonic to the diatonic v, the classic I → v tonic-to-minor-fifth-degree jump. *And Your Bird Can Sing* E → Bm and *Helter Skelter* E → Bm are cited in the same family, and the early A Hard Day’s Night / A Hard Day’s Night-type I → v gestures in G are the same vocabulary.

On the interval / ♭V reading that the wording “minor fifth” most naturally evokes, *Come Together* is the canonical, most repeatedly named Beatles opening. On the scale-degree / v reading the canonical exemplar is *Norwegian Wood*.

3.text:
The I – v jump that is taught as the Beatles’ “tonic to the minor fifth” is the diatonic
I → v root motion, i.e. tonic to the minor triad built on the fifth degree of the
major key.

That is the opening of Norwegian Wood – This Bird Has Flown.

The song is set up in E major. The sitar / guitar intro states the tonic E major
and the first vocal phrase is set over it

* I once had a girl…     E  major  I

The harmony then moves straight to the diatonic minor fifth degree on the
continuation of the line

* …or should I say…      B minor  v

E → Bm is a perfect-fifth root motion, tonic to the minor chord on the fifth
degree of the key, the classic I → v tonic-to-minor-fifth opening that is
normally cited together with I Feel Fine / Helter Skelter / And Your Bird Can
Sing, E major → B minor, and in G major with A Hard Day’s Night / All My
Loving / I Saw Her Standing There, G major → E minor.

It is the diatonic I–v form of the move.  If the “minor fifth” is taken in the
strict intervallic sense i.e. a tritone / bV, the same descriptive family is the
Beatles’ I → bV tritone openings, the canonical textbook example being the
E → B♭/G♯ tritone area of Come Together and the C → G♭/F♯ I→bV of
Happiness Is a Warm Gun / I Want You (She’s So Heavy), with A Day In The
Life G → E♭ being the verse illustration.

6.text:
The split in the room is basically a terminological split.

If you mean a diatonic I → v move, i.e. tonic to the minor triad built on the 5th degree, a perfect-fifth root movement with a minor quality, the example that is actually in the literature is the E → Bm opening of *Norwegian Wood [This Bird Has Flown]* and essentially the same E → Bm gesture that is quoted for *And Your Bird Can Sing*.  That is I → v, perfect fifth root movement, minor quality on the fifth degree.  The same gesture is what is taught for the early “tonic to v” material and is correctly identified for *Norwegian Wood*.

If you mean what is normally called a “minor fifth” interval in the English rock-theory literature, i.e. a six-semitone / tritone root jump tonic → ♭V, then you are not after a diatonic v at all.  The clearest textbook Beatles illustration of an actual tonic-to-minor-fifth / tonic-to-tritone jump at the very start of the record is the White Album C → G♭ opening.

That is the opening of *I Want You [She’s So Heavy]*, and the same C → G♭ / I → ♭V material is the one quoted for the opening section of *Happiness Is a Warm Gun*. In C the band states a tonic C major and the next harmony brought in is the G♭-major/minor sonority a diminished 5th / minor 5th, six semitones, away from C.  The same I–♭V tritone archetype is the one that is normally invoked for *Come Together* in E, the E tonic being immediately answered by the E–B♭/G♯ tritone / ♭V area of the famous riff, and for the A → E♭ tritone opening of *Strawberry Fields Forever*.

That is why *Come Together / I Want You [She’s So Heavy] / Strawberry Fields Forever* keep recurring in the ♭V/tritone reading, whereas *Norwegian Wood* / *And Your Bird Can Sing* recurring in the I→v perfect-fifth minor-quality reading.  On the usual “minor fifth = tritone” reading the canonical opening is the I → ♭V tritone jump of *Come Together*, exemplified in the clearest form by *I Want You [She’s So Heavy]* C → G♭.

1.text:
The interval that is normally called a “minor fifth’’ in interval nomenclature is six semitones, i.e. the tritone / diminished fifth. A root move of six semitones up from the tonic is not I–v, which is a perfect fifth in the root, it is I–♭V.

The two families you are mixing are therefore not the same.

* I → v = tonic to the diatonic minor triad built on the fifth degree. 
The root move is a perfect 5th, 7 semitones. E→Bm, A→Em, G→Em etc. That is the
‘tonic-to-the-minor-fifth-degree’ move that is quoted for Norwegian Wood,
And Your Bird Can Sing, Helter Skelter, A Hard Day’s Night etc. Norwegian Wood
is the textbook E major → B minor example, but E–B is a perfect fifth in the
root, not a minor fifth.

* I → ♭V = tonic to a chord whose root is a minor fifth / tritone away from the
tonic. That is the move that is normally described in the literature as the
Beatles’ tonic-to-minor-fifth / tonic-to-tritone jump.

The canonical first-bar instance of that is Come Together.

The number is set up in E, the tonic E major being stated by drums/bass/rhythm
guitar at the downbeat, and the riff/harmony that is immediately heard against
it is the tritone-related ♭V area, E → B♭/G♯. It is routinely glossed as the
Beatles’ I → ♭V, tonic to minor-fifth / tritone, opening. The same
I–♭V/tri tone colour is the one that is quoted for the White Album material
I Want You – She’s So Heavy / Happiness Is a Warm Gun C → G♭/F♯, Strawberry
Fields Forever A → E♭/G♭ and the verse of A Day in the Life G → E♭.

If the question is taken strictly as an intervallic minor fifth / tritone root
move the textbook example is Come Together, E → B♭, with I Want You –
She’s So Heavy C → G♭ and Happiness Is a Warm Gun C → F♯ as the same
class. If you meant the diatonic ‘minor fifth-degree’ v chord, the interval
in the root is a perfect fifth and the most often cited exemplar is
Norwegian Wood – This Bird Has Flown, E major → B minor, i.e. I → v.

5.text:
The tonic → minor-fifth root movement that is taught as a Beatles signature is the
tritone / ♭V root jump, i.e. a root movement of a diminished/minor fifth, six
semitones, and the canonical illustration of that is the introduction of
*Come Together*.

In the studio recording the band is set up in E. The rhythm guitar and drums
establish an E-major tonic area and the first melodic/bass statement of the
famous riff is heard against that E tonic reference. The harmonic centre that
is immediately sensed next is the tritone-related area a minor fifth / six
semitones away from E, the E–B♭/G♯ sonority, conventionally glossed as
E → B♭, i.e. I → ♭V. It is that E tonic – B♭/bV tritone leap which gives the
introduction its characteristic ‘wrong’ jump and which is routinely quoted
in the literature as the Beatles’ textbook tonic-to-minor-fifth / I–bV opening.

That is the same class of move that is quoted for the other Sgt. Pepper/White
Album tritone openings – A → E♭ in *Strawberry Fields Forever*, C → G♭/F♯ in
*Happiness Is a Warm Gun* / *I Want You (She’s So Heavy)* and G → E♭ in the
verse of *A Day In The Life* – and it is the form in which the “minor-fifth’’
interval is normally taught as a root movement.

If the phrase “minor fifth chord’’ is taken in the strictly diatonic major-key
sense, i.e. the triad built on the fifth scale degree, v, the textbook
Beatles I→v example that is most repeatedly cited in the room is the
E-major → B-minor opening of *Norwegian Wood (This Bird Has Flown)*,
and by the same gesture *And Your Bird Can Sing*, with the E → Bm I→v move
also quoted for *Helter Skelter*/*I Feel Fine* material.  That is the diatonic
v reading of the question; the tritone/♭V reading is the Come Together/
Strawberry Fields/Happiness Is a Warm Gun family.

4.text:
The terminology is the whole problem.

If you take “minor-fifth chord” strictly as an interval, i.e. a root motion of a diminished 5th / tritone, I → ♭V, then the textbook Beatles example that is quoted in the literature is the opening of Come Together, and the same class of move is the White Album C → G♭/F♯ opening of Happiness Is a Warm Gun / I Want You (She’s So Heavy).

Come Together is set up in E. The rhythm guitar / drums establish an E major tonic reference and the first melodic/bass statement of the riff is heard as E immediately answered by the tritone-related ♭V area, the E → B♭/G♯ E–B♭ tritone / minor-fifth root motion that colours the whole introduction. That is the move that is routinely glossed in the rock literature as the Beatles’ I → ♭V / tonic-to-minor-fifth / tonic-to-tritone jump. The same I – ♭V tritone jump is the one that is normally cited for the C major opening of Happiness Is a Warm Gun, C tonic answered by the F♯/G♭ tritone area, and that is the material the I Want You (She’s So Heavy) intro re-uses.

If you are using “minor fifth chord” in the lay / diatonic sense = the minor triad built on the fifth degree of the tonic, I → v, then you are talking about a perfect-fifth root motion to a diatonic v. That class is most often illustrated with Norwegian Wood (This Bird Has Flown), whose verse is taught as E major tonic → B minor v, E → Bm, the same I–v gesture that is also quoted for And Your Bird Can Sing E → Bm and for the early rock-and-roll I–v openings such as A Hard Day’s Night G → Em/Dm. That is the I → v “tonic to the minor fifth-degree chord” reading.

On the strict interval reading the canonical, unambiguously documented example is Come Together; on the diatonic v reading the canonical example most repeatedly cited in the group is Norwegian Wood E → Bm.

8.text:
The wording “tonic to the minor-fifth chord” is normally used in the Beatles literature for the tonic-to-tritone / tonic-to-♭V root motion, i.e. a six-semitone/minor-fifth / ‘minor fifth’ interval at the root, not for the diatonic v.

On that reading the textbook White Album example is C → G♭/F♯.

*Happiness Is a Warm Gun* is written in C major. The vocal entry “I need a fix…” is introduced over a tonic C major triad and is answered immediately by the harmony whose root is a tritone/minor fifth away from C, the F♯/G♭ area heard in the recording as F♯ major/minor colour. In conventional terms that is I → ♭V, the tonic to the minor-fifth / tritone substitution that gives the opening its characteristic ‘wrong’ jump. The same C → G♭/F♯ material is the one that is normally quoted for the introduction of *I Want You (She’s So Heavy)*, the White Album C–G♭ tritone that is taught as the classic tonic-to-♭5 / tonic-to-minor-5th root motion.

That is the same class of move that is quoted for *Come Together* E → B♭/G♯ and for *Strawberry Fields Forever* A → E♭/G♭.

If the question is taken in the strictly diatonic sense I → v, tonic to the minor triad built on the fifth degree, the canonical early-mid period example that is repeatedly cited in the same discussion is the E major → B minor opening of *Norwegian Wood (This Bird Has Flown)*, and the same I–v gesture is the one normally illustrated by *And Your Bird Can Sing* E → Bm and by the A/G → E minor family *I Saw Her Standing There/All My Loving*.

9.text:
The “tonic → minor fifth” gloss is being used in the literature in two different ways and the two families have to be kept distinct.

* I → v  = tonic to the diatonic minor triad built on the fifth degree of the key, a perfect-fifth root motion. On that reading the canonical Beatles I → v openings are the E → Bm openings that are quoted again and again: Norwegian Wood – This Bird Has Flown, And Your Bird Can Sing, Helter Skelter, I Feel Fine, etc., and the G → Em/A Hard Day’s Night family. That is the I → v “tonic to the minor fifth-degree chord” reading.

* I → ♭V / I → tritone  = tonic to a chord whose root is a minor fifth / 6 semitones / tritone above the tonic. On that reading the phrase “minor fifth chord’’ is an interval description, not a scale-degree description.

It is the second, interval reading that is normally taught as the Beatles’ textbook “tonic to the minor-fifth/tritone’’ jump and it is the one that is normally meant by “chord jump from the tonic to the minor fifth chord”.

The textbook instance is *Come Together*.

The number is set up in E. The rhythm guitar/drum set up is heard as an E tonic area and the first melodic/harmonic statement of the Lennon bass riff is heard against it as the tritone-related area E → B♭/G♯, i.e. I → ♭V, the minor fifth / diminished fifth / tritone root motion. E–B♭ is six semitones, a minor fifth, and that is the dissonant tonic-to-tritone launch that colours the whole introduction and is the one most often illustrated in rock theory as the Beatles’ classic I → ♭V/minor-fifth jump.

The same I → ♭V tritone family is what is being cited for *Happiness Is a Warm Gun / I Want You (She’s So Heavy)* C → G♭/F♯, *Strawberry Fields Forever* A → E♭/G♭ and the *A Day In The Life* G → E♭ verse. *Come Together* is the most repeatedly quoted of those as the archetypal tonic-to-minor-fifth/tritone opening.

If the question is taken in the diatonic scale-degree sense I → v, the exemplar that is most often quoted is the E → Bm opening of *Norwegian Wood – This Bird Has Flown* – and the same I → v gesture is the one usually cited for *And Your Bird Can Sing* and *Helter Skelter*.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the key issue is that several of us are conflating two different musical ideas: a **minor-fifth chord** (the v chord, a minor triad on scale degree 5) and a **flat-fifth/tritone** (♭V). The question asks for the former, not the latter. That makes *Norwegian Wood* the cleanest fit: it is in E major, the opening establishes E as tonic, and the first real harmonic/vocal move goes to B minor — E → Bm, I → v. That is exactly a tonic-to-minor-fifth-chord jump, with no enharmonic or chord-quality ambiguity.

The tritone-based candidates — *Come Together*, *Happiness Is a Warm Gun*, *I Want You*, *A Day in the Life* — are being justified through I–♭V/tritone language, which is not the same as I–v. *Strawberry Fields Forever* is also being described in that A–E♭/G♭ tritone way, so its current rationale doesn’t actually establish the minor-fifth chord move we’re looking for. *A Hard Day’s Night* has the famous ambiguous opening sonority and key/chord disputes, so it’s much less clean as a textbook I–v example. If we want the unambiguous case, *Norwegian Wood* is the one: E major to B minor at the outset.

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the key is to keep “minor fifth chord” strictly as the diatonic **v** chord—the minor triad built on the fifth degree—not the flattened fifth/tritone that several of us have been invoking. That distinction clears up a lot of the confusion: it rules out the I–♭V/tritone candidates like *Come Together*, *Helter Skelter*, *I Want You (She’s So Heavy)*, *Happiness Is a Warm Gun*, and *A Day in the Life*, because those are not tonic-to-v movements in the sense the question seems to ask.

Among the clean I–v openings, *Norwegian Wood (This Bird Has Flown)* is still the strongest. The song is in E, and the first real harmonic shift is E major to B minor—tonic to the minor fifth—at the opening vocal phrase. The move is immediate, diatonic, and textbook: E → Bm, I → v. That is exactly what the wording describes, without needing to reinterpret “minor fifth” as a tritone.

The *A Hard Day’s Night* claims are less secure: the opening chord is famously ambiguous/overloaded, and the D minor reading is not as clean or uncontested as the E → Bm move in *Norwegian Wood*. As for *Strawberry Fields Forever*, C2’s rationale actually gives A → E♭/G♭, which is a tritone/♭V, not a minor fifth chord. If we take “minor fifth” seriously as v, that argument undercuts itself rather than supporting *Strawberry Fields*. So I’d consolidate around *Norwegian Wood* as the clearest and most defensible I–v opening.

The interval that is normally called a “minor fifth’’ in interval nomenclature is six semitones, i.e. the tritone / diminished fifth. A root move of six semitones up from the tonic is not I–v, which is a perfect fifth in the root, it is I–♭V.

The two families you are mixing are therefore not the same.

* I → v = tonic to the diatonic minor triad built on the fifth degree. 
The root move is a perfect 5th, 7 semitones. E→Bm, A→Em, G→Em etc. That is the
‘tonic-to-the-minor-fifth-degree’ move that is quoted for Norwegian Wood,
And Your Bird Can Sing, Helter Skelter, A Hard Day’s Night etc. Norwegian Wood
is the textbook E major → B minor example, but E–B is a perfect fifth in the
root, not a minor fifth.

* I → ♭V = tonic to a chord whose root is a minor fifth / tritone away from the
tonic. That is the move that is normally described in the literature as the
Beatles’ tonic-to-minor-fifth / tonic-to-tritone jump.

The canonical first-bar instance of that is Come Together.

The number is set up in E, the tonic E major being stated by drums/bass/rhythm
guitar at the downbeat, and the riff/harmony that is immediately heard against
it is the tritone-related ♭V area, E → B♭/G♯. It is routinely glossed as the
Beatles’ I → ♭V, tonic to minor-fifth / tritone, opening. The same
I–♭V/tri tone colour is the one that is quoted for the White Album material
I Want You – She’s So Heavy / Happiness Is a Warm Gun C → G♭/F♯, Strawberry
Fields Forever A → E♭/G♭ and the verse of A Day in the Life G → E♭.

If the question is taken strictly as an intervallic minor fifth / tritone root
move the textbook example is Come Together, E → B♭, with I Want You –
She’s So Heavy C → G♭ and Happiness Is a Warm Gun C → F♯ as the same
class. If you meant the diatonic ‘minor fifth-degree’ v chord, the interval
in the root is a perfect fifth and the most often cited exemplar is
Norwegian Wood – This Bird Has Flown, E major → B minor, i.e. I → v.

The terminology is the whole problem.

If you take “minor-fifth chord” strictly as an interval, i.e. a root motion of a diminished 5th / tritone, I → ♭V, then the textbook Beatles example that is quoted in the literature is the opening of Come Together, and the same class of move is the White Album C → G♭/F♯ opening of Happiness Is a Warm Gun / I Want You (She’s So Heavy).

Come Together is set up in E. The rhythm guitar / drums establish an E major tonic reference and the first melodic/bass statement of the riff is heard as E immediately answered by the tritone-related ♭V area, the E → B♭/G♯ E–B♭ tritone / minor-fifth root motion that colours the whole introduction. That is the move that is routinely glossed in the rock literature as the Beatles’ I → ♭V / tonic-to-minor-fifth / tonic-to-tritone jump. The same I – ♭V tritone jump is the one that is normally cited for the C major opening of Happiness Is a Warm Gun, C tonic answered by the F♯/G♭ tritone area, and that is the material the I Want You (She’s So Heavy) intro re-uses.

If you are using “minor fifth chord” in the lay / diatonic sense = the minor triad built on the fifth degree of the tonic, I → v, then you are talking about a perfect-fifth root motion to a diatonic v. That class is most often illustrated with Norwegian Wood (This Bird Has Flown), whose verse is taught as E major tonic → B minor v, E → Bm, the same I–v gesture that is also quoted for And Your Bird Can Sing E → Bm and for the early rock-and-roll I–v openings such as A Hard Day’s Night G → Em/Dm. That is the I → v “tonic to the minor fifth-degree chord” reading.

On the strict interval reading the canonical, unambiguously documented example is Come Together; on the diatonic v reading the canonical example most repeatedly cited in the group is Norwegian Wood E → Bm.

The “tonic → minor fifth” gloss is being used in the literature in two different ways and the two families have to be kept distinct.

* I → v  = tonic to the diatonic minor triad built on the fifth degree of the key, a perfect-fifth root motion. On that reading the canonical Beatles I → v openings are the E → Bm openings that are quoted again and again: Norwegian Wood – This Bird Has Flown, And Your Bird Can Sing, Helter Skelter, I Feel Fine, etc., and the G → Em/A Hard Day’s Night family. That is the I → v “tonic to the minor fifth-degree chord” reading.

* I → ♭V / I → tritone  = tonic to a chord whose root is a minor fifth / 6 semitones / tritone above the tonic. On that reading the phrase “minor fifth chord’’ is an interval description, not a scale-degree description.

It is the second, interval reading that is normally taught as the Beatles’ textbook “tonic to the minor-fifth/tritone’’ jump and it is the one that is normally meant by “chord jump from the tonic to the minor fifth chord”.

The textbook instance is *Come Together*.

The number is set up in E. The rhythm guitar/drum set up is heard as an E tonic area and the first melodic/harmonic statement of the Lennon bass riff is heard against it as the tritone-related area E → B♭/G♯, i.e. I → ♭V, the minor fifth / diminished fifth / tritone root motion. E–B♭ is six semitones, a minor fifth, and that is the dissonant tonic-to-tritone launch that colours the whole introduction and is the one most often illustrated in rock theory as the Beatles’ classic I → ♭V/minor-fifth jump.

The same I → ♭V tritone family is what is being cited for *Happiness Is a Warm Gun / I Want You (She’s So Heavy)* C → G♭/F♯, *Strawberry Fields Forever* A → E♭/G♭ and the *A Day In The Life* G → E♭ verse. *Come Together* is the most repeatedly quoted of those as the archetypal tonic-to-minor-fifth/tritone opening.

If the question is taken in the diatonic scale-degree sense I → v, the exemplar that is most often quoted is the E → Bm opening of *Norwegian Wood – This Bird Has Flown* – and the same I → v gesture is the one usually cited for *And Your Bird Can Sing* and *Helter Skelter*.

I think the key issue is that several of us are conflating two different musical ideas: a **minor-fifth chord** (the v chord, a minor triad on scale degree 5) and a **flat-fifth/tritone** (♭V). The question asks for the former, not the latter. That makes *Norwegian Wood* the cleanest fit: it is in E major, the opening establishes E as tonic, and the first real harmonic/vocal move goes to B minor — E → Bm, I → v. That is exactly a tonic-to-minor-fifth-chord jump, with no enharmonic or chord-quality ambiguity.

The tritone-based candidates — *Come Together*, *Happiness Is a Warm Gun*, *I Want You*, *A Day in the Life* — are being justified through I–♭V/tritone language, which is not the same as I–v. *Strawberry Fields Forever* is also being described in that A–E♭/G♭ tritone way, so its current rationale doesn’t actually establish the minor-fifth chord move we’re looking for. *A Hard Day’s Night* has the famous ambiguous opening sonority and key/chord disputes, so it’s much less clean as a textbook I–v example. If we want the unambiguous case, *Norwegian Wood* is the one: E major to B minor at the outset.

I think the key is to keep “minor fifth chord” strictly as the diatonic **v** chord—the minor triad built on the fifth degree—not the flattened fifth/tritone that several of us have been invoking. That distinction clears up a lot of the confusion: it rules out the I–♭V/tritone candidates like *Come Together*, *Helter Skelter*, *I Want You (She’s So Heavy)*, *Happiness Is a Warm Gun*, and *A Day in the Life*, because those are not tonic-to-v movements in the sense the question seems to ask.

Among the clean I–v openings, *Norwegian Wood (This Bird Has Flown)* is still the strongest. The song is in E, and the first real harmonic shift is E major to B minor—tonic to the minor fifth—at the opening vocal phrase. The move is immediate, diatonic, and textbook: E → Bm, I → v. That is exactly what the wording describes, without needing to reinterpret “minor fifth” as a tritone.

The *A Hard Day’s Night* claims are less secure: the opening chord is famously ambiguous/overloaded, and the D minor reading is not as clean or uncontested as the E → Bm move in *Norwegian Wood*. As for *Strawberry Fields Forever*, C2’s rationale actually gives A → E♭/G♭, which is a tritone/♭V, not a minor fifth chord. If we take “minor fifth” seriously as v, that argument undercuts itself rather than supporting *Strawberry Fields*. So I’d consolidate around *Norwegian Wood* as the clearest and most defensible I–v opening.

So I’d consolidate on *Come Together* as the textbook I→♭V / tonic-to-minor-fifth opening, and treat the v-reading as the fallback interpretation. 1.text:
The split continues to be purely terminological and it is the only thing that is still moving the discussion.

On standard interval nomenclature a minor fifth = 6 semitones = diminished fifth = tritone. A root move of a minor fifth up from the tonic is therefore I → ♭V, not I → v. I → v is a perfect fifth root motion, 7 semitones, tonic to the diatonic minor triad built on scale degree 5.

That interval reading is the one the Beatles rock-theory literature uses when it talks about a “tonic to the minor fifth / tonic to the tritone” opening.

On that reading the canonical first-bar instance is *Come Together*.

The track is set up in E. Drums, rhythm guitar and McCartney’s bass establish an E-major tonic reference at the downbeat and the Lennon bass/riff that is immediately heard against it is the tritone-related ♭V area E → B♭/G♯. E–B♭ is six semitones, a minor fifth/diminished fifth/tritone, i.e. I → ♭V.

That is the textbook tonic-to-minor-fifth/tritone jump that is routinely glossed as the Beatles’ archetypal tonic-to-minor-fifth opening. The same I → ♭V / tritone class is what is quoted for the White Album material *I Want You – She’s So Heavy / Happiness Is a Warm Gun* C → G♭/F♯, *Strawberry Fields Forever* A → E♭/G♭ and the verse of *A Day in the Life* G → E♭, with *Come Together* as the most repeatedly named archetype.

*Norwegian Wood – This Bird Has Flown* E major → B minor, *And Your Bird Can Sing* E → Bm and the G → Em family are textbook I → v, tonic to the minor triad on the fifth scale degree. The root motion there is a perfect fifth, 7 semitones. It is the cleanest exemplar of the diatonic “tonic to the minor fifth-degree chord” reading, but it is not a minor-fifth interval in the root.

If “minor fifth chord” is taken in the strict intervallic sense in which the phrase is normally used in the literature, the answer the question intends is the I → ♭V tritone launch of *Come Together* E → B♭/G♯, with *I Want You – She’s So Heavy / Happiness Is a Warm Gun* C → G♭ as the clearest White Album illustration of the same family. The I → v reading is *Norwegian Wood* E → Bm, and that is the best answer only if the question setter is using “minor fifth chord” in the lay scale-degree sense = the minor triad on scale degree 5.
